newsitem.title: USA: White House official testifies in Whitewater case.
newsitem.headline: White House official testifies in Whitewater case.

text.p: A senior White House official denied before a grand jury on Thursday that former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell was given "hush money" for his silence in the Whitewater investigation.

Thomas "Mack" McLarty, a White House counsellor and the president's former chief of staff, said he had no sinister motives in helping Hubbell find work after Hubbell resigned from his Justice Department post in 1994.

"I was attempting to help a friend and colleague in a time of need. What I did seemed to me to be the right thing. That's the way I was raised," McLarty told reporters after testifying for eight hours before a Whitewater grand jury in Little Rock.

Hubbell, once a close friend of President Clinton, resigned amid controversy over his private law practice in early 1994 and later that year pleaded guilty to fraudulent billing of clients at the Rose Law Firm in Little Rock before he joined the Clinton administration. He was jailed in 1995.

McLarty and current White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles made phone calls on Hubbell's behalf in the months after his resignation, but both men insist they were unaware at that point of his illegal acts and deny suggestions they were helping to buy Hubbell's silence.
"Had Webb been truthful (about the investigation against him), I would have acted differently," McLarty said Thursday.
Bowles testified before the same federal grand jury on Tuesday, and also denied that Hubbell was paid to keep quiet on Clinton's role in Whitewater.
Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr is trying to determine whether the jobs provided to Hubbell after he left the Justice Department were intended to buy his silence.
Clinton has said he saw nothing improper about the calls and that both Bowles and McLarty were simply showing "human compassion" for a man with four children who was out of work.
Hubbell has denied withholding information that might damage the president and first lady.

James McDougal, Clinton's former partner in the failed Whitewater real estate venture that lies at the centre of the scandal, was sentenced to only three years in prison on Monday after agreeing to cooperate with Starr's investigators. He had faced up to 81 years in prison.
